Nanda’s observance of the precepts is fully detailed as recorded in the fourth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.

Regarding the Pratyekabuddha, it merely explains the causes for attaining the fruit and the excellence of the Dharma sought; however, if one follows the analogy of the Śrāvaka, the specific characteristics of their practice must also be clarified, and so forth.

The passage beginning with "If there is a son of the Buddha" opens the Mahāyāna of the six perfections; the cultivation of various practices and supreme wisdom is common to all teachings. Now, although at the initial stage one resembles ordinary beings or those of the Small Vehicle, they still obtain the names "various" and "supreme," and because these are not mixed with the ordinary or the Small Vehicle, it is collectively termed "pure."
Regarding "not ultimately pure": for the time being, speaking in terms of the Tripiṭaka and the Six Pāramitās, it is called "pure" simply because there is no disease within the medicine.

If one wishes to distinguish the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) herein: "the different practices of the Three Vehicles" refers to the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly purpose); "Pratyekabuddha" refers to the *puruṣakāra* (personal benefit); "Śrāvaka" refers to the *pratipakṣa* (remedy); and "Bodhisattva" refers to the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth). Moreover, since each of these individually possesses all four *siddhāntas*, the application of these principles to the teachings of the Three Vehicles can be understood by analogy.
The contemplation of the fundamental and the trace (honjaku kanjin) should likewise be understood; the various *pāramitās* that follow shall be briefly explained according to the text.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, the śrāvakas," etc., this is stated for the time being according to one specific path within the respective teaching (*jiō*). It should be understood that in the Shared Teaching (*tsūkyō*), the three vehicles all take the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) within the realm of conditioned existence as their initial gateway; in the Distinct Teaching (*betsukyō*), the Bodhisattvas take the Path Truth (*mārga-satya*) outside the realm of conditioned existence as their initial gateway; and those of the Perfect Teaching (*enkai*) take the Truth of Cessation outside the realm of conditioned existence as their initial gateway.

In this context, since one has seen [the truth] momentarily through the light of the cause, it is not appropriate to seek the characteristics of phenomena extensively; rather, a brief indication that they accord with principle is sufficient. If one discusses actual practice, then they may be analyzed in detail.
The following thirty-one lines and a half extensively clarify the two flavors; therefore, this passage is judged to belong solely to the Tripiṭaka.

Regarding the phrase "concluding the former and opening the latter": when it concludes the preceding discussion by mentioning "seeing, hearing, and matters," it refers to both the gradual and sudden teachings, as they all speak of "expounding" and "preaching for others," which constitutes "hearing."
The phrase "Furthermore, one sees the sons of the Buddha," and so forth, refers to the act of seeing.
Within this seeing, the various manifold elements are all phenomena (*vastu*).
Because the general outline is sufficiently established, it says "in such a manner" (*evam*); that which is common is abbreviated, referring here to thousands of millions of phenomena.

Regarding the phrase "opening up what follows," it is called "now I shall" because it continues the subsequent discourse; furthermore, it is placed within the text concerning the thousand billion matters, and now both [aspects] should be drawn together.

Furthermore, the first four lines may serve to conclude what precedes, while the two lines beginning with "In this way" open up what follows; thus, the metaphor of the orchid and the chrysanthemum finds its proper application here.

The thirty-one and a half lines that follow are divided into sections simply titled "The Bodhisattva’s Cultivation. Since these passages occur after [the teaching at] the Deer Park and before the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, one should—according to the subsequent explanation of the *Prajñāpāramitā*—understand them as encompassing both "milk" and "cream," for the characteristics of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* have not yet been definitively resolved. Therefore, they are explained with deliberate care.
Although the two types of *sūtra* (the *Sūtra* and the *Vaipulya*) are mentioned, the teaching primarily concerns the three [vehicles], as distinguished previously.

Regarding the various *pāramitās* in relation to the teachings, prior to the *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) [teachings], they generally do not mention "teaching," as this encompasses two meanings.

The subsequent explanation of the meaning follows the general structure of the section to provide a clear overview, as the prose text explicitly states that it concerns the *Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā*. Regarding the term "Ganges sands" (*gaṅgā-vāluka*) mentioned in the general inquiry:

from the four sides of Lake Anavatapta, a river issues from each. From the silver bull-mouth in the east flows the Gaṅgā River; from the golden elephant-mouth in the south flows the Sindhu River; from the lapis lazuli horse-mouth in the west flows the Vakṣu River; and from the crystal lion-mouth in the north flows the Sītā River. Each river circles the lake once before flowing into one of the four oceans.

Among them, the Gaṅgā is subtle yet numerous; non-Buddhists reckon it to be a river of merit, entering which one washes away sins, and the Buddha, conforming to worldly custom, frequently refers to it.
Furthermore, because the Buddha frequently taught the Dharma near this river, it is used as a metaphor.

The following discussion of the six perfections merely provides a brief indication of their general essence; if one were to fully elaborate on their characteristics according to the two flavors [of the teachings], it would be exactly as cited in the second and seventh records of the *Zhiguan*.
Question:
Since it is said that the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā should also contain both teachings and the two vehicles, how can you ask in general about seeking only the Buddha-way?
Answer:
It is indeed as you have asked; however, to avoid prolixity and because it would otherwise be the same as [the teaching at] the Deer Park, I have omitted it here.
As for "four horses," they are called *sì* (a team of four) because four horses are yoked together to pull a carriage.
The character "xiá" (俠) is pronounced like *hú tié* (胡帖); it means a "heroic figure" (*háo*).

Regarding the phrase "went to visit" (*wǎng yì*) and so forth in the *Sūtra* under the term "Mañjuśrī": it indicates that he went specifically to the Buddha’s abode and not elsewhere. Since that which was inquired about is the most supreme, it is called the "Unsurpassed Way" (*anuttara-mārga*); since that which was abandoned is not something trivial, it is called a "Land of Bliss" (*sukhāvatī*); and since both body and mind are detached from [worldly things], it is said "shaved off" (*tì chú*).
Thus, in explaining what is commonly shared by the world, all commentaries value the core of the teaching; the refinement of revealing the principle lies in pruning away its redundancies.
The *Pañcarājāsūtra* is a short scripture consisting of a single fascicle.
A sutra states:

"In the past, there were five kings whose neighboring countries did not compete with one another, and who were mutual friends. One great king was named Pujian (Universal Peace); he practiced the bodhisattva path. Because the other four kings were filled with rampant false views, Pujian took pity on them, summoned them to his palace, and provided them with entertainment and pleasure for seven days and seven nights.
The four kings said, 'Our state affairs are many; we request to return home.'"
The Great King personally escorted them and commanded his attendants to accompany them.
When they had traveled halfway, he questioned them, saying:
"What does each of you find pleasing?"
One said: "I wish to roam the wilds on a day of spring sunshine.
The other said:
"May I always be a king, adorned with various ornaments, with the people and attendants on the roads casting their eyes upward in admiration.
Another said:
"May I obtain a fine wife and sons who are peerlessly handsome."
One said: "I pray that my parents may live long and have many brothers, and that we may all enjoy ourselves together with fine food and music.
After each had spoken thus, they turned to address the Great King:
"What is Your Majesty's wish?
He replied,
"I have already stated that your wish is not long-lasting."

If one delights in spring excursions, one will first wither and decay in winter; if one delights in being a king, one will be attacked when merit is exhausted; if one delights in wife and children, one will suffer immeasurable pain from illness in a single morning; if one delights in parents remaining forever, they will suddenly be seized by others when misfortune strikes.
The Four Kings asked again:
"Great King, what is it that you delight in?
He replied:
"What I delight in is neither arising nor ceasing, neither suffering nor pleasure, neither hunger nor thirst, neither cold nor heat;
it is the mastery over both existence and non-existence. The Four Kings asked: "Where does such a joy exist?"
"Where is the Teacher?
The Great King replied, "My Teacher is named Buddha; he is nearby at the Jetavana."
The kings were filled with joy and each went to the Buddha’s dwelling; withdrawing to sit on one side, they addressed the Buddha and reproached themselves.

The Buddha preached the eight sufferings, and the king along with his retinue of hundreds of thousands of people attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; they abandoned their kingdoms to enter the Path, their great circumstances being largely the same.

Since it is stated that he inquired after the Unsurpassed Way, this does not concern the minor fruits [of the Śrāvaka]; however, because the matter of abandoning his land and leaving home is the same, I have cited it here.

While what was seen within the light may also take the eight sufferings as auxiliary practices—since this is common to all teachings and thus the abandonment of national affairs is the same—the contemplative practice must be distinguished in order to differentiate between the various teachings.
Furthermore, as in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, there were four wheel-turning kings who divided a single kingdom and hired people to shave their heads;
since it says "the capacities of the various kings were not uniform," the subsequent passage beginning with "furthermore, he saw" and so forth also applies to these various capacities.
